stem:
A researcher records the time (in minutes) that 40 customers spend in a coffee shop. The distribution of times is strongly right-skewed, with a few customers staying much longer than typical. The five-number summary is: Min = 3, Q1 = 8, Median = 12, Q3 = 18, Max = 65.

Which measure of center and spread is most appropriate to report for this distribution, and why?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mean and standard deviation, because they use every data value in the distribution.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mean and range, because the range captures the full spread including the long visits.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Median and IQR, because they are resistant to the strong right skew and the high outlier.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Median and standard deviation, because the median is resistant but the shape of the distribution doesn't affect measures of spread.

rationales.A: Both the mean and standard deviation are pulled toward the long right tail and the high outlier (65); they are not resistant, so 'uses every value' is not a reason to prefer them for a skewed distribution.
rationales.B: The range is determined entirely by the two most extreme values, making it even more sensitive to the outlier than the standard deviation; the mean is also not resistant.
rationales.C: The median and IQR depend only on the middle portion of the ordered data, so they are not distorted by the skew or the outlier at 65 minutes -- the standard choice for a skewed distribution.
rationales.D: This mixes a resistant measure of center with a non-resistant measure of spread; shape and outliers affect standard deviation just as much as they affect the mean.

stem:
On a nationally normed exam, scores are approximately normally distributed with mean 500 and standard deviation 100. Fatima scores 640. On a different, unrelated diagnostic test with mean 20 and standard deviation 4, Diego scores 26.

Which student performed better relative to their own test's distribution, and by how many standard deviations above the mean?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Diego, because his z-score of 1.5 is higher than Fatima's z-score of 1.4.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fatima, because 640 is a higher raw score than 26.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fatima, because her raw score is farther from her test's mean (140 points) than Diego's is from his (6 points).

choices.label: D
choices.text: The two students performed identically, because both scored above their test's mean.

rationales.A: Fatima's z-score is (640 - 500)/100 = 1.4. Diego's z-score is (26 - 20)/4 = 1.5. Standardizing puts both scores on the same scale, and Diego's is higher.
rationales.B: Comparing raw scores directly ignores that the two tests have completely different means and standard deviations; raw scores from different distributions are not comparable without standardizing.
rationales.C: Comparing raw point distances from the mean ignores the different scales (standard deviations) of the two tests; 140 points on a test with SD 100 is less extreme than 6 points on a test with SD 4.
rationales.D: Both scoring above the mean does not mean the performances are equivalent; the magnitude of each score's standardized distance from the mean still needs to be compared.

stem:
A wellness magazine reports that people who meditate at least 20 minutes per day have lower blood pressure on average than people who do not meditate, based on a survey of 500 adults who volunteered to report their meditation habits and blood pressure.

Which conclusion is appropriately supported by this study design?

choices.label: A
choices.text: There is an association between meditation habits and blood pressure in this sample, but causation cannot be concluded because participants were not randomly assigned to meditate or not.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Meditating for 20 minutes a day causes lower blood pressure.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because the sample size is large (500 people), causation can be concluded even without random assignment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No conclusion can be drawn because the study did not use a randomized experiment.

rationales.A: This was an observational, voluntary-response study with no random assignment of the explanatory variable, so an association can be described but a causal claim is not supported.
rationales.B: This draws a causal conclusion from an observational study with no random assignment, which cannot rule out confounding variables.
rationales.C: A large sample size reduces sampling variability but does nothing to address confounding; only random assignment supports causal claims.
rationales.D: This overcorrects -- observational studies can still support conclusions about association, just not causation.

stem:
A researcher wants to test whether a new fertilizer increases tomato plant yield compared to a standard fertilizer. She has 40 tomato plants: 20 grown in full-sun plots and 20 grown in partial-shade plots. She plans to randomly assign fertilizer type (new vs. standard) separately within the full-sun group and separately within the partial-shade group, rather than randomizing across all 40 plants at once.

What is the primary statistical benefit of this design compared to completely randomizing fertilizer type across all 40 plants without regard to sun exposure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It removes the need for random assignment altogether, since sun exposure is already controlled.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It guarantees that the new fertilizer will outperform the standard fertilizer within each sun-exposure group.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It reduces variability in yield due to sun exposure, making it easier to detect a true difference between fertilizers if one exists.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It increases the sample size available for comparing the fertilizers.

rationales.A: Blocking does not replace random assignment; fertilizer type is still randomly assigned within each sun-exposure block.
rationales.B: Blocking controls a source of variability; it does not guarantee any particular outcome for either treatment.
rationales.C: Blocking by a known nuisance variable (sun exposure) removes its variability from the comparison between fertilizers, increasing the power to detect a real treatment effect.
rationales.D: Blocking reorganizes how the same 40 plants are grouped and randomized; it does not add any additional plants or observations.

stem:
A vending machine dispenses two independent snack items in a bundle. The number of chip bags dispensed has mean 3 and standard deviation 0.8. The number of candy bars dispensed has mean 2 and standard deviation 0.6. Let T = total number of snack items (chips + candy) dispensed in a bundle.

What is the standard deviation of T?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 1.4, because standard deviations of independent random variables add directly.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 0.2, because the standard deviation of a sum is the difference of the standard deviations.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 1.96, because the variance of T is the square of the sum of the two standard deviations.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 1.0, because Var(T) = 0.8^2 + 0.6^2 = 0.64 + 0.36 = 1.00, so SD(T) is the square root of 1.00.

rationales.A: Standard deviations do not add directly, even for independent random variables; it is the variances that add.
rationales.B: This applies the wrong operation entirely; subtracting standard deviations has no statistical justification here.
rationales.C: This squares the sum of the standard deviations (0.8 + 0.6)^2 instead of summing the individual variances, a common algebra-of-variance error.
rationales.D: For independent random variables, variances add: Var(T) = Var(chips) + Var(candy) = 0.64 + 0.36 = 1.00, so SD(T) = sqrt(1.00) = 1.0.

stem:
The distribution of individual household incomes in a large city is strongly right-skewed. A researcher plans to take a random sample of n households and compute the sample mean income, x-bar.

As the sample size n increases from 10 to 100, what happens to the shape and variability of the sampling distribution of x-bar?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The shape becomes more skewed and the variability increases, matching the population more closely as n grows.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The shape stays exactly as skewed as the population, but the variability decreases.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The shape becomes more normal and the variability (standard error) decreases.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The shape becomes more normal, but the variability stays the same regardless of n.

rationales.A: This reverses both effects of the Central Limit Theorem; larger samples make the sampling distribution of the mean look less like the skewed population, not more.
rationales.B: This ignores the Central Limit Theorem's effect on shape; as n increases, the sampling distribution of x-bar becomes more normal, not equally skewed.
rationales.C: The Central Limit Theorem states that as n increases, the sampling distribution of x-bar becomes more approximately normal regardless of population shape, and its standard error (population SD divided by the square root of n) decreases as n increases.
rationales.D: This correctly describes the shape change but incorrectly claims the standard error is unaffected by sample size, when in fact it decreases as n increases.

stem:
A quality control engineer wants to use a normal approximation for the sampling distribution of the sample proportion of defective items in a random sample of size n = 40 from a manufacturing process where the true defect rate is p = 0.03.

Why is it inappropriate to use a normal approximation for the sampling distribution of p-hat in this situation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: np = 40(0.03) = 1.2, which is less than 10, so the success-failure condition is not met and the sampling distribution of p-hat would be skewed, not approximately normal.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The sample size 40 is too small to ever use a normal approximation, regardless of p.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The population defect rate p = 0.03 is a parameter, not a statistic, so the normal approximation does not apply to parameters.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Random sampling was not used, so no approximation is valid.

rationales.A: The success-failure condition requires both np and n(1-p) to be at least 10 (a common threshold); here np = 1.2, which fails the condition, so the normal approximation is not justified.
rationales.B: Appropriateness depends on np and n(1-p), not on the sample size n alone; a sample of 40 could be adequate for a different value of p.
rationales.C: This confuses the parameter/statistic distinction with the actual condition being checked; the success-failure condition uses p to check np and n(1-p), regardless of p being a parameter.
rationales.D: The stimulus states the sample is random; this introduces an assumption violation that isn't actually present in the scenario.

stem:
A polling organization constructs a 95% confidence interval for the proportion of adults in a state who support a new transportation initiative and obtains the interval (0.46, 0.54) based on a random sample of 800 adults.

Which is a correct interpretation of this confidence interval?

choices.label: A
choices.text: There is a 95% probability that the true population proportion is between 0.46 and 0.54.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 95% of adults in the state support the initiative, plus or minus 4 percentage points.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If this exact sample were surveyed 100 times, the sample proportion would fall between 0.46 and 0.54 ninety-five times.

choices.label: D
choices.text: We are 95% confident that the interval from 0.46 to 0.54 captures the true proportion of all adults in the state who support the initiative, based on the method used to construct it.

rationales.A: The true population proportion is a fixed (though unknown) number, not a random variable, so it is incorrect to assign a probability to it falling in a specific interval.
rationales.B: This confuses the confidence interval for the unknown population proportion with a statement about what fraction of individual adults support the initiative.
rationales.C: "95% confidence" describes the long-run behavior of the method across many different random samples, not repeated surveys of the same fixed sample.
rationales.D: This correctly ties the 95% confidence level to the reliability of the interval-construction method over repeated random sampling, rather than to a probability statement about the fixed parameter.

stem:
A nutritionist wants to construct a confidence interval for the mean sugar content (in grams) of a population of energy bars using a random sample of 8 bars. A dotplot of the 8 sample values shows a strong right skew with one bar much higher in sugar content than the rest.

Is it appropriate to construct a one-sample t-interval for the mean using this sample?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No, because the sample size is small (n = 8) and the sample data show strong skewness, so there is no good reason to believe the sampling distribution of x-bar is approximately normal.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes, because the sample was randomly selected, and random selection is the only condition required for a t-interval.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes, because the Central Limit Theorem guarantees the sampling distribution of x-bar is approximately normal for any sample size greater than 5.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No, because t-intervals can never be used with sample sizes smaller than 30.

rationales.A: With a small sample and clear skewness/an outlier in the data, there is no basis for assuming the population is approximately normal or that the sampling distribution of the mean is approximately normal, so the t-interval's normality condition is not satisfied.
rationales.B: Random selection is one condition, but the normal/large-sample condition on the shape of the data or the sampling distribution must also be checked; it is not the only requirement.
rationales.C: There is no such rule; the Central Limit Theorem's normal approximation improves gradually with sample size and depends on how skewed the population is, not a fixed cutoff of 5.
rationales.D: This overgeneralizes a common rule of thumb into an absolute rule; small samples can still support a t-interval when there's good reason to believe the population itself is approximately normal, which is not the case here given the observed skew.

stem:
A researcher collects data on eye color (categorized as Brown, Blue, Green, Hazel, or Other) for a random sample of 60 people from a small town, wanting to test whether the town's eye-color distribution matches known national percentages. After computing expected counts under the national percentages, the expected count for the "Other" category is 2.4, while all other categories have expected counts above 10.

What is the best course of action given this situation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Proceed with the chi-square goodness-of-fit test as planned; expected counts do not need to meet any minimum threshold as long as the observed counts are all positive.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Combine the "Other" category with another sparse or conceptually similar category so that all expected counts are at least 5, then proceed with the chi-square goodness-of-fit test using the reduced set of categories.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Switch to a chi-square test for independence instead, since that test has no minimum expected-count requirement.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increase the significance level from 0.05 to 0.10 to compensate for the small expected count in the "Other" category.

rationales.A: Chi-square procedures require expected counts to meet a minimum threshold (commonly at least 5 in each category) for the chi-square approximation to be valid; observed counts being positive does not address this.
rationales.B: Combining categories to raise low expected counts to at least 5 is the standard way to satisfy the expected-counts condition while still allowing a valid chi-square goodness-of-fit test to proceed.
rationales.C: The expected-counts condition applies to chi-square procedures generally, including tests for independence and homogeneity; switching tests does not remove the requirement.
rationales.D: Adjusting the significance level addresses the decision threshold, not the underlying condition violation caused by a too-small expected count; it does not fix the validity problem.

stem:
Using the same study as the previous item (n = 45 adults, slope b = -1.8, SE(b) = 0.6), a t-test of H0: beta = 0 versus Ha: beta does not equal 0 produces a p-value of 0.004. This was an observational study; adults were not randomly assigned their exercise habits.

Which is the correct conclusion at alpha = 0.05?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Because p = 0.004 is less than 0.05, there is convincing evidence of a negative linear relationship between hours of exercise and resting heart rate in the population, but since this was an observational study, causation cannot be concluded from this test alone.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because p = 0.004 is less than 0.05, there is convincing evidence that increasing exercise causes a decrease in resting heart rate.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because p = 0.004 is less than 0.05, the null hypothesis is proven false and beta must equal -1.8 in the population.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because p = 0.004 is less than 0.05, there is convincing evidence of a strong linear relationship, meaning r-squared must be close to 1.

rationales.A: The small p-value gives convincing evidence against beta = 0, supporting a real linear association in the population, but because adults were not randomly assigned their exercise habits, confounding variables cannot be ruled out and a causal claim is not supported.
rationales.B: This draws a causal conclusion from an observational study with no random assignment of exercise habits, which cannot rule out confounding variables such as age or overall fitness.
rationales.C: Rejecting a null hypothesis provides evidence against beta = 0; it does not "prove" the null false with certainty, nor does it establish that the population slope equals the sample estimate exactly.
rationales.D: Statistical significance (driven partly by sample size) and effect size (such as r-squared) are different concepts; a small but real slope can be highly statistically significant with a large enough sample without indicating a strong r-squared.

stem:
A set of delivery times is strongly right-skewed, with a few very long times.

Which pair of summary statistics is most appropriate to describe the center and spread?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mean and standard deviation, because they use all the data values.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mean and range, because the range captures the overall spread.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Median and IQR, because they are resistant to the skew and the long right tail.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Median and standard deviation, because the median is resistant.

rationales.A: Using every value is not an advantage when the distribution is skewed; these measures are not resistant.
rationales.B: The range is driven only by the extreme values and is extremely sensitive to outliers.
rationales.C: Median and IQR are resistant measures, so they are the standard choice for skewed distributions and outliers.
rationales.D: This mixes a resistant center with a non-resistant spread measure.

stem:
A test has mean 70 and standard deviation 8.

What is the z-score for a student who scored 78?

rationales.A: This subtracts the mean but does not standardize by the standard deviation.
rationales.C: This divides by 10 instead of 8 or treats the difference incorrectly.
rationales.D: The sign is wrong; 78 is above the mean.

stem:
A data set has 12 values with mean 40. One value is changed from 18 to 30.

How does the mean change?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It increases by 12.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It does not change.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It increases by 0.5.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It increases by 1.0, because the total sum increases by 12 and the data set has 12 values.

rationales.A: That is the change in one data value, not the change in the mean.
rationales.B: Changing a data value changes the mean unless the change is zero.
rationales.C: This divides by the wrong number of values.
rationales.D: Changing one value by +12 raises the mean by 12/12 = 1.

stem:
A boxplot has a long right whisker and one high outlier.

Which description best matches the distribution?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Right-skewed with a high outlier.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Left-skewed with a low outlier.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Approximately symmetric with no outliers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Bimodal with two clusters.

rationales.A: A long right whisker and a high outlier indicate right skew.
rationales.B: This describes the opposite tail behavior.
rationales.C: The long right tail and outlier contradict symmetry.
rationales.D: A boxplot does not by itself show two modes, and nothing here indicates bimodality.

stem:
Data values are 10, 11, 12, 12, 13, 13, 15, 40.

Which measure is most resistant to the outlier 40?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Range

choices.label: B
choices.text: Standard deviation

choices.label: C
choices.text: IQR

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mean

rationales.A: The range is entirely determined by the minimum and maximum, so it is not resistant.
rationales.B: Standard deviation is pulled by extreme values and is not resistant.
rationales.C: IQR depends on the middle half of the ordered data and is resistant to a single extreme value.
rationales.D: The mean is also not resistant to outliers.

stem:
A data set has 20 observations ordered from least to greatest.

Which statement about the median is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The median is the 10th value only.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The median is the average of the 10th and 11th values.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The median is the difference between the 10th and 11th values.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The median is the mean of all 20 values.

rationales.A: That would be true only for an odd number of observations.
rationales.B: For an even number of observations, the median is the average of the two middle values.
rationales.C: Median is an average, not a difference.
rationales.D: That describes the mean, not the median.

stem:
For a data set, Q1 = 18 and Q3 = 30.

What is the upper fence for possible outliers?

rationales.A: This uses 1.0(IQR) instead of 1.5(IQR).
rationales.B: This mistakenly starts from Q1 instead of Q3: Q1 + 1.5(IQR) = 18 + 1.5(12) = 18 + 18 = 36.
rationales.C: This doubles Q3 instead of adding 1.5×IQR to it: 2 × Q3 = 2(30) = 60.
rationales.D: IQR = 12, so the upper fence is Q3 + 1.5(IQR) = 30 + 18 = 48.

stem:
A score is at the 75th percentile on a test.

What does that mean?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 75% of scores are at or below that score.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The score is 75 points higher than the mean.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 75% of scores are above that score.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The score is the average of the top 75% of scores.

rationales.A: Percentiles describe the percentage of observations at or below the given value.
rationales.B: Percentile does not measure distance from the mean.
rationales.C: That would describe the 25th percentile, not the 75th.
rationales.D: That is not what a percentile means.

stem:
A distribution is roughly symmetric with no outliers.

Which statement is most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The mean must be much larger than the median.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The median must always be larger than the mean.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The mean and median will be close to each other.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The range is always the best measure of spread.

rationales.A: That would suggest right skew, not symmetry.
rationales.B: There is no such rule.
rationales.C: In a roughly symmetric distribution, mean and median tend to be similar.
rationales.D: The best measure depends on shape and outliers.

stem:
A teacher wants a random sample of 30 students from a list of 300.

What is the best method?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Choose the first 30 students in alphabetical order.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Choose only students who volunteer.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Assign each student a number and use a random number generator to select 30 numbers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Choose every student whose birthday is in January.

rationales.A: This is not random and may be biased.
rationales.B: Volunteers create voluntary-response bias.
rationales.C: A simple random sample gives every student an equal chance of being selected.
rationales.D: This is systematic by a nonrandom rule and may be biased.

stem:
A school has freshmen, sophomores, juniors, and seniors in different proportions.

Why might stratified sampling be better than a simple random sample?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It ensures each grade level is represented in the sample.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It guarantees no bias under any circumstance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It always requires fewer people than any other method.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It removes the need for random selection.

rationales.A: Stratified sampling can improve representativeness when important subgroups need guaranteed representation.
rationales.B: No sampling method guarantees zero bias.
rationales.C: Sample size depends on the precision desired, not just the method.
rationales.D: Strata are typically sampled randomly within each group.

stem:
Researchers record whether students study music and whether they prefer online lectures. They do not assign any treatment.

What type of study is this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Randomized experiment

choices.label: B
choices.text: Case-control experiment

choices.label: C
choices.text: Double-blind trial

choices.label: D
choices.text: Observational study

rationales.A: No random assignment or imposed treatment is described.
rationales.B: This is not an experimental design.
rationales.C: No treatment or blinding is described.
rationales.D: The researchers only observe existing behavior and do not impose a treatment.

stem:
An experiment compares two diets, but age may affect results.

How could blocking help?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ignore age because random assignment always eliminates all variation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Group subjects into age categories before random assignment within each age block.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Use convenience sampling instead.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Use the largest age group only.

rationales.A: Random assignment reduces confounding but does not remove all variation.
rationales.B: Blocking controls a known source of variability by balancing it across treatments.
rationales.C: Convenience sampling increases bias and does not block anything.
rationales.D: This would discard data and does not properly block.

stem:
A study finds that students who sleep more also score higher on tests.

Which is a plausible confounding variable?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The regression slope

choices.label: B
choices.text: The sample size

choices.label: C
choices.text: Study habits or prior preparation

choices.label: D
choices.text: The p-value

rationales.A: The slope is part of the analysis, not a lurking variable.
rationales.B: Sample size affects precision, not the causal mechanism in the same way.
rationales.C: A third variable could affect both sleep and test scores, producing the observed association.
rationales.D: The p-value is a summary of evidence, not a confounder.

stem:
A school randomly assigns students to a new tutoring program or the old program.

What does random assignment help with most?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Guaranteeing a perfectly equal sample size in every subgroup.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Eliminating all measurement error.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Making the study automatically double blind.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Balancing lurking variables between the groups so a causal comparison is more credible.

rationales.A: Random assignment does not guarantee equal subgroup sizes.
rationales.B: Random assignment does not fix measurement problems.
rationales.C: Blinding is separate from random assignment.
rationales.D: Random assignment helps create comparable groups and supports causal inference.

stem:
A survey is conducted only by texting students with smartphones.

What bias is most likely?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Undercoverage bias

choices.label: B
choices.text: Response bias only

choices.label: C
choices.text: No bias because texting is random.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Placebo effect

rationales.A: Students without smartphones are systematically left out of the sample frame.
rationales.B: The main issue is that some students are excluded before response occurs.
rationales.C: The sample frame is not representative of all students.
rationales.D: Placebo effects apply to experiments, not surveys.

stem:
A medical trial is designed so neither the subjects nor the evaluators know who receives the pill or placebo.

Why is this useful?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It guarantees the treatment works.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It helps reduce placebo effects and observer bias.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It removes the need for random assignment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It makes the sample larger.

rationales.A: Blinding does not guarantee effectiveness.
rationales.B: Blinding reduces the chance that expectations affect responses or measurements.
rationales.C: Random assignment is still needed.
rationales.D: Blinding does not change sample size.

stem:
A principal asks every student in the school to fill out a survey.

What is this called?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A random sample

choices.label: B
choices.text: A stratified sample

choices.label: C
choices.text: A census

choices.label: D
choices.text: A biased sample

rationales.A: Not everyone is selected randomly when all are surveyed.
rationales.B: There is no subsampling by strata here.
rationales.C: A census collects data from every member of the population of interest.
rationales.D: A census may still have nonresponse issues, but it is still a census by definition.

stem:
In a class of 40 students, 10 are athletes, and 4 of those athletes are on the honor roll.

What is P(honor roll | athlete)?

rationales.A: Conditional probability uses the athlete group as the denominator.
rationales.B: This uses the whole class instead of only the athletes.
rationales.C: This is P(athlete), not the conditional probability.
rationales.D: This incorrectly uses the number of athletes NOT on the honor roll (10 − 4 = 6) as the denominator instead of all 10 athletes: 4/6 ≈ 0.67.

stem:
P(A) = 0.3, P(B) = 0.4, and P(A and B) = 0.12.

Are A and B independent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No, because P(A) and P(B) are not equal.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No, because the events both have probabilities less than 1.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes, because A and B cannot both happen.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes, because P(A)P(B) = 0.12 = P(A and B).

rationales.A: Equal probabilities are not required for independence.
rationales.B: All probabilities are less than 1; that does not determine independence.
rationales.C: That would describe mutually exclusive events, not independence.
rationales.D: Independence holds when the joint probability equals the product of the marginal probabilities.

stem:
A two-stage process has P(first success) = 0.3 and P(second success | first success) = 0.5.

What is the probability of success on both stages?

rationales.A: This adds probabilities instead of multiplying along the path.
rationales.B: Multiply along the path: 0.3 × 0.5 = 0.15.
rationales.C: This combines the numbers incorrectly.
rationales.D: This is not the probability of the joint path.

stem:
A game pays $10 with probability 0.2 and $0 otherwise.

What is the expected value?

rationales.A: This is the prize amount, not the expected value.
rationales.B: This is 10 × 0.8, which uses the wrong probability.
rationales.D: There is a positive probability of winning, so the expected value is not zero.

stem:
The probability that it rains tomorrow is 0.25.

What is the probability that it does not rain?

rationales.A: Use the complement: 1 - 0.25 = 0.75.
rationales.B: This repeats the original probability instead of its complement.
rationales.C: This is not the complement of 0.25.
rationales.D: This does not sum with 0.25 to 1.

stem:
A single card is drawn from a standard deck.

Can the card be both a heart and a spade?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Yes, because all suits overlap.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes, if the card is red.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No, because the events are independent.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No, because those events are mutually exclusive.

rationales.A: Suits are distinct categories.
rationales.B: Red does not make a card both a heart and a spade.
rationales.C: Mutually exclusive is the relevant idea, not independence.
rationales.D: One card cannot belong to two different suits at the same time.

stem:
A basketball player makes a free throw with probability 0.7 on each attempt.

What features are needed for a binomial setting?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any random experiment with numerical outcomes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A fixed number of trials, independent trials, two outcomes per trial, and a constant success probability.

choices.label: C
choices.text: At least three outcomes on each trial.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A changing success probability from trial to trial.

rationales.A: Not every random experiment is binomial.
rationales.B: Those are the standard binomial conditions.
rationales.C: Binomial trials have only two outcomes.
rationales.D: Constant p is required.

stem:
A club wants to choose 3 officers from 10 members, with no order.

Which counting method is appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Permutation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Multiplication rule only

choices.label: C
choices.text: Combination

choices.label: D
choices.text: Binomial distribution

rationales.A: Permutation counts ordered arrangements, which is not needed here.
rationales.B: That alone does not account for choosing without order.
rationales.C: When order does not matter, use combinations.
rationales.D: This is a counting situation, not a binomial probability setting.

stem:
P(A) = 0.6, P(B) = 0.5, and P(A and B) = 0.2.

What is P(A or B)?

rationales.A: Use the addition rule: P(A or B) = 0.6 + 0.5 - 0.2 = 0.9.
rationales.B: This subtracts too much or omits one event.
rationales.C: This adds the probabilities without correcting for overlap.
rationales.D: This is only the intersection.

stem:
A population has σ = 12 and samples of size n = 36 are taken.

What is the standard error of x̄?

rationales.A: This is the population standard deviation, not the standard error.
rationales.C: This is √n, not the standard error.
rationales.D: This is not a valid SE computation.

stem:
A population is strongly skewed, but n = 50 random samples are taken.

Why is the sampling distribution of x̄ often approximately normal?

choices.label: A
choices.text: By the Central Limit Theorem, large samples tend to produce an approximately normal sampling distribution of x̄.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because every population is normal when n = 50.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because the sample mean always equals the population mean.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because skewness disappears in the raw data.

rationales.A: The CLT says the sampling distribution of the mean becomes approximately normal as n grows large.
rationales.B: The population itself does not become normal.
rationales.C: The sample mean varies from sample to sample.
rationales.D: The raw data can still be skewed.

stem:
A 95% confidence interval for a population proportion has margin of error 0.04.

What happens if the sample size increases and all else stays the same?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The margin of error gets larger.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The margin of error stays exactly the same.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The margin of error gets smaller.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The margin of error becomes negative.

rationales.A: That is the opposite of the sample-size effect.
rationales.B: Sample size affects SE and MOE.
rationales.C: Larger samples reduce standard error, which shrinks the margin of error.
rationales.D: Margins of error are never negative.

stem:
Two samples are taken from the same population, one with n = 25 and one with n = 100.

Which sample has the smaller standard error?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The sample with n = 25.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The sample with n = 100.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both samples have the same SE.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neither sample has an SE.

rationales.A: Smaller samples have larger standard error.
rationales.B: SE decreases as n increases because the denominator √n gets larger.
rationales.C: Sample size changes the SE.
rationales.D: Every sample mean has a standard error in this context.

stem:
A new estimator consistently misses the true value by a large amount, even with large samples.

What is the main problem?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Only variability

choices.label: B
choices.text: Normality

choices.label: C
choices.text: Independence

choices.label: D
choices.text: Bias

rationales.A: Large random scatter is not the only issue when the estimator is consistently off target.
rationales.B: Normality is not the central issue described here.
rationales.C: The question is about systematic error, not dependence.
rationales.D: If an estimator is systematically off target, the estimator is biased.

stem:
A sample proportion uses p̂ with p = 0.4 and n = 100.

What is the standard error of p̂?

rationales.B: This is the numerator p(1-p), not the standard error.
rationales.C: This is the proportion, not its standard error.
rationales.D: This is 1-p, not the standard error.

stem:
A study has β = 0.25 for a particular test.

What is the power of the test?

rationales.A: That is β, the Type II error rate.
rationales.B: Power = 1 - β = 0.75.
rationales.C: That would be α in many settings, not power.
rationales.D: This is not 1 - β here.

stem:
A test gives p-value = 0.018 and α = 0.05.

What should the statistical decision be?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fail to reject H₀ because the p-value is not zero.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Accept H₀ as proven true.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ignore the p-value and use the sample mean only.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reject H₀; the result is statistically significant at the 0.05 level.

rationales.A: A p-value does not need to be zero to reject the null.
rationales.B: We do not prove the null hypothesis true.
rationales.C: Inference is based on the p-value and significance level.
rationales.D: Since p < α, the evidence is strong enough to reject the null hypothesis.

stem:
A survey of 200 people finds 118 support a policy. The question is whether support exceeds 50%.

Which hypotheses are correct?

rationales.A: Null and alternative are reversed.
rationales.B: The claim is that support exceeds 50%, so this is a right-tailed test for a proportion.
rationales.C: This uses the wrong parameter symbol.
rationales.D: Proportions are not counts.

stem:
The same 20 students are measured before and after a study program.

Which procedure is most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A paired t procedure on the differences.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A two-sample t procedure for independent samples.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A two-proportion z test.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A one-proportion z test.

rationales.A: The same individuals are measured twice, so the data are paired.
rationales.B: The samples are not independent because they come from the same students.
rationales.C: The data are quantitative, not categorical.
rationales.D: This procedure is for a single categorical proportion, not for paired quantitative differences.

stem:
Two studies test the same hypothesis, but one has a much larger sample size.

Which study is more likely to have greater power, all else equal?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The study with the smaller sample size.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The study with the larger sample size.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They must have the same power.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Power depends only on the p-value.

rationales.A: Smaller samples usually have less power.
rationales.B: Larger samples reduce SE and usually make it easier to detect a true effect.
rationales.C: Sample size affects power.
rationales.D: Power is about the test design and true effect, not the observed p-value alone.

stem:
A table shows 30 of 100 students prefer the new app.

What is the marginal probability that a student prefers the app?

rationales.A: 30 out of 100 students prefer the app, so the marginal probability is 0.30.
rationales.B: This is the probability of not preferring the app.
rationales.C: This incorrectly divides by 1000 or uses the wrong scale.
rationales.D: That would require 50 students, not 30.

stem:
A factory has three machines with different defect rates and production shares.

Which formula correctly finds P(machine B | defective)?

choices.label: A
choices.text: P(B)P(defective)

choices.label: B
choices.text: P(B | defective) = P(B) / P(defective | B)

choices.label: C
choices.text: P(defective | B) + P(B)

choices.label: D
choices.text: P(defective | B)P(B) / P(defective)

rationales.A: This is not conditional probability; it omits the denominator.
rationales.B: That is not Bayes’ theorem.
rationales.C: Probabilities are not combined this way.
rationales.D: Bayes’ theorem reverses the conditional probability using the defect probability in the numerator and the total defect probability in the denominator.

stem:
A student wants to test whether preference for a snack is related to grade level using a contingency table.

Which procedure is appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chi-square goodness-of-fit

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chi-square test of independence

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two-sample t test

choices.label: D
choices.text: Paired t test

rationales.A: Goodness-of-fit is for one categorical variable and one distribution.
rationales.B: Two categorical variables from one sample are being tested for association.
rationales.C: t tests are for means, not categorical counts.
rationales.D: The data are not paired quantitative measurements.

stem:
A chi-square table cell has row total 40, column total 50, and grand total 200.

What is the expected count in the cell?

rationales.A: This adds the row and column totals instead of using the expected-count formula: 40 + 50 = 90.
rationales.B: This uses half the grand total as the denominator: (40×50)/100 = 20.
rationales.C: Expected count = (row total × column total) / grand total = 40×50/200 = 10.
rationales.D: This uses double the grand total as the denominator: (40×50)/400 = 5.

stem:
A binomial setting has n = 5 and p = 0.5.

What is P(X = 0)?

rationales.A: That is the probability of a single success, not zero successes in five trials.
rationales.C: This is not the correct binomial calculation for zero successes.
rationales.D: That is the trial count, not a probability.

stem:
A researcher wants SE = 2 when σ = 10.

What sample size is needed?

rationales.A: This confuses the square root of n with n itself.
rationales.B: This does not satisfy 10/√n = 2.
rationales.C: This would make the SE smaller than 2.
rationales.D: SE = σ/√n, so 2 = 10/√n gives √n = 5 and n = 25.

stem:
A test reports p = 0.12 and α = 0.05.

Which conclusion is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reject H₀ because p is less than 1.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Accept H₀ as proven.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fail to reject H₀; the result is not statistically significant at the 0.05 level.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The alternative hypothesis is true with probability 0.12.

rationales.A: Any p-value is less than 1, but that does not imply significance.
rationales.B: We do not prove the null true.
rationales.C: Because p > α, the evidence is not strong enough to reject the null.
rationales.D: That is a common misinterpretation of p-values.

stem:
A random variable takes values 1, 2, and 3 with probabilities 0.2, 0.5, and 0.3.

What is the mean?

rationales.B: This likely comes from a rough average rather than the weighted mean.
rationales.C: This is not the correct weighted average.
rationales.D: This is the largest outcome, not the mean.

stem:
A 95% CI for a regression slope is (0.4, 1.2).

What can you conclude?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The slope is significantly different from 0 at the 0.05 level because the interval does not include 0.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The slope must equal 0.8 exactly.

choices.label: C
choices.text: There is no linear relationship.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The intercept is between 0.4 and 1.2.

rationales.A: A CI for a slope that excludes 0 indicates evidence of a linear relationship.
rationales.B: A confidence interval gives a range of plausible values, not a single guaranteed value.
rationales.C: Excluding 0 suggests evidence of a linear relationship.
rationales.D: This is a slope interval, not an intercept interval.

stem:
A null hypothesis is rejected even though it is actually true.

What type of error occurred?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Type II error

choices.label: B
choices.text: Type I error

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sampling error

choices.label: D
choices.text: No error

rationales.A: Type II error is failing to reject a false null hypothesis.
rationales.B: A Type I error is rejecting a true null hypothesis.
rationales.C: This is a more general term, not the specific hypothesis-test error.
rationales.D: Rejecting a true null hypothesis is an error.

stem:
A slope test gives p = 0.008 for H₀: β = 0.

What is the strongest correct conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The slope is exactly 0.008.

choices.label: B
choices.text: There is no evidence of a relationship because 0.008 is small.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The correlation must be 0.008.

choices.label: D
choices.text: There is convincing evidence of a linear relationship between x and y in the population, but causation is not justified without random assignment.

rationales.A: A p-value is not the slope estimate.
rationales.B: Small p-values are evidence against H₀.
rationales.C: p-values and correlations are different quantities.
rationales.D: A small p-value supports a nonzero slope, but causation requires more than observational regression evidence.

stem:
Two studies test the same claim, but one uses a more stringent significance level and a smaller sample size.

Which study is most likely to have lower power?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The study with the smaller sample size and more stringent α.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The study with the larger sample size and more stringent α.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The study with the larger sample size and larger α.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both studies must have the same power.

rationales.A: Lower α and smaller n both tend to reduce power.
rationales.B: Larger n increases power, all else equal.
rationales.C: Larger α increases power.
rationales.D: Power depends on n and α, so they need not match.

stem:
A 99% confidence interval is wider than a 95% confidence interval from the same sample.

Why?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Because the sample mean changes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A higher confidence level uses a larger critical value, which makes the interval wider.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because the standard deviation becomes larger.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because 99% means less certainty than 95%.

rationales.A: The same sample was used; the critical value changed.
rationales.B: More confidence requires a wider interval to capture the parameter more often in the long run.
rationales.C: The sample standard deviation does not change just because confidence level changes.
rationales.D: 99% confidence is more, not less, confidence.

stem:
A randomized experiment compares two study methods and collects quantitative exam scores.

Which statement best combines design and inference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Because it is a randomized experiment, any sample difference proves causation with no additional conditions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because the data are quantitative, causation cannot be discussed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because of random assignment, a significant difference in sample means supports a causal conclusion in context if the inference conditions are met.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because p-values measure the size of the effect, causation is automatic.

rationales.A: Inference conditions still matter.
rationales.B: Randomized experiments can support causal conclusions.
rationales.C: Random assignment supports causation; significance supports a difference in means if conditions hold.
rationales.D: p-values indicate evidence, not effect size.

stem:
A slope CI for study hours vs exam score is entirely positive.

What does this suggest?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The response variable must be categorical.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The slope is definitely exactly the midpoint of the interval.

choices.label: C
choices.text: There is evidence of a negative slope.

choices.label: D
choices.text: There is evidence that the population slope is positive, so more study time is associated with higher predicted scores.

rationales.A: The response in regression remains quantitative.
rationales.B: The midpoint is a point estimate, not a guaranteed true slope.
rationales.C: An interval entirely above 0 indicates a positive slope, not a negative one.
rationales.D: A CI entirely above 0 indicates a positive slope in the population.

stem:
Two independent samples compare support for a policy: group 1 has 58 of 100 supporters, group 2 has 70 of 125 supporters.

Which inference procedure is appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A two-proportion z procedure.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A paired t procedure

choices.label: C
choices.text: A one-sample t procedure

choices.label: D
choices.text: A chi-square goodness-of-fit test

rationales.A: Two independent categorical groups with success/failure outcomes call for a two-proportion z procedure.
rationales.B: The samples are not paired and the response is categorical.
rationales.C: The response is not quantitative.
rationales.D: The question compares two groups, not one distribution to a claimed distribution.
